title: 50 years on from Arts Britain Ignores: how much has changed for black and Asian artists?
summary:
Conference to explore legacy of Naseem Khan’s seminal 1976 report on the exclusion of minority ethnic artists

It is 50 years since cultural historian Naseem Khan’s challenge to the British…

blocks.text: It is 50 years since cultural historian Naseem Khan’s challenge to the British arts establishment was first published, and the question of who and what counts as British continues to be contested.

The Arts Britain Ignores – Khan’s groundbreaking 1976 report, commissioned by organisations including the then Arts Council of Great Britain, presented a vision of a pluralistic national culture, in which the creativity of Britons of diverse ethnic backgrounds – from bhangra music, to black painters and Ukrainian dance – should be recognised, supported and respected.

Today, when polls, debates and cultural and political moments present differing notions of British identity – whether it is the diversity of the England football team, or how political figures choose to define their own identities – Khan’s work retains its relevance.

blocks.caption: Undated photo of Naseem Khan. Photograph: Frank Martin/The Guardian

blocks.text: On Wednesday, Dawn Airey, the new chair of cultural funding and development agency Arts Council England, will give her inaugural speech at a conference celebrating Khan’s legacy – The Arts Britain Ignores: 50 Years On – at Serendipity Institute for Black Arts and Heritage in Leicester.

Today, the work of black and Asian British visual artists, such as Frank Bowling, Sonia Boyce and Anish Kapoor is critically acclaimed and in demand. But in 1976, Khan documented how grassroot arts and cultural practices that thrived in UK ethnic minority communities were largely ignored by funders and critics.

This week’s conference, bringing together artists, organisations, experts and policymakers, will explore how much progress has been made in 50 years and comes at a time when community and independent cultural spaces face pressures over finances, redevelopment and gentrification.

blocks.caption: Dancer and choreographer Tebandeke Joseph performing in TimeMachine at Let’s Dance International Frontiers 2026. Photograph: Leesha Williams

blocks.text: Contributors to Wednesday’s conference include Khan’s daughter, Amelia Torode, the theatre director Jatinder Verma, the broadcaster Brenda Emmanus and the crossbench peer and chancellor of the University of Nottingham, Lola Young.

blocks.caption: Cover of the new book The Arts Britain Ignores: 50 Years On. Photograph: Serendipity Institute for Black Arts and Heritage / The Unloved.

blocks.text: The conference also marks the launch of a new book, The Arts Britain Ignores at 50, published by Serendipity Institute, including essays and new research.

Pawlet Brookes, the chief executive and artistic director of Serendipity Institute, said: “We had Cool Britannia, we’ve had the ‘ain’t no black in the union jack’. We’ve had all of that narrative. But the reality is British is diverse – whether that diversity is layered with colour or layered in other ways. We can go down a negative road, or we can celebrate what we have, which is fantastic, the best in Europe – although we still have some way to go.”

blocks.caption: British-Indian sculptor Anish Kapoor next to his installation Mount Moriah at the Gate of the Ghetto at the Hayward Gallery, London, in June. Photograph: Chris J Ratcliffe/Reuters

blocks.text: Describing Khan’s work as “seminal”, Brookes said it was time to “see how far we’ve travelled, and what we need to do for the next 50 years.”

She added: “We did a timeline investigation [for the new book] and what it shows is that, there has been funding for culturally diverse organisations, but what there hasn’t been is sustainability and growth.
“We also need recognition for dance and theatre, in the way that progress has been made in the visual arts.”

blocks.caption: The artist Frank Bowling at the launch of his  exhibition Seeking the Sublime, at the Fitzwilliam Museum in Cambridge, in March. Photograph: Joe Giddens/PA

blocks.text: In her speech, Airey is expected to say: “The journey Khan set us on remains one of the most important our sector is undertaking … [it] will sit at the centre of my work.”

She praises Khan as having told institutions such as the Arts Council that “you have built an entire cultural establishment – its funding structures, its buildings, its critics, its canon – around a definition of British art that leaves whole swathes of it out.”

blocks.caption: Dawn Airey, the new chair of Arts Council England, will be speaking at the conference. Photograph: Gary Calton/The Guardian

blocks.text: Airey is also expected to say: “It a hard time to be an artist in this country, whatever your background – but for many people in this room it is harder still.

“Racism, Islamophobia and antisemitism are part of daily life for too many people in our sector: sometimes in crude and obvious ways, sometimes in subtle and deniable ones, but constantly there … So let me be emphatic. Those of us who don’t experience this – and I include myself – have a responsibility to stand with you: to stand up for the work you want to make, and to back that with action, not just words.”
